title: Python basics
short: Names, the few value types, and what counts as true.
what: A variable is a name that points at a value: x = 7. You never declare a type; the value carries it. Interviews use only a handful: int, float, str, bool and None.
analogy: A sticky note with a name on it. x = 7 sticks the note "x" on the number 7. Stick it on "hi" later and x now means "hi".

frames.label: x = ...
frames.say: x = 7 makes an int. No type is written: the value decides it. 3.5 is a float, "hi" a str, True a bool.

frames.label: x = ...
frames.say: None means "no value yet" and has its own type. 0, the empty string and the empty list are real values too.

frames.label: if x: ... runs?
frames.say: Inside an if, every value counts as true or false. Non-zero numbers, non-empty strings and True count as true.

frames.label: if x: ... runs?
frames.say: None, 0, "" and [] count as false. So "if nums:" reads as "if the list is not empty".

frames.label: a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]; c = a
frames.say: a = [1, 2] and b = [1, 2] hold equal lists, so a == b is True. == compares the values inside.

frames.label: a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]; c = a
frames.say: But they are two separate lists, so a is b is False. is asks "the very same object?". c = a shares the object.

frames.label: best = 0 is a real answer
frames.say: Use is only for None: if best is None. Then a real answer of 0 is not mistaken for "no answer yet".

when: Check if a list or string is empty
Compare two values, or ask if two names share one object
python:
x = 7
y = 3.5
name = "hi"
print(type(x), type(y), type(name), type(True))
for v in [7, 0, "hi", "", [1], [], None]:
    print(repr(v), bool(v))
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b, c is a)
best = 0
if best is not None:
    print("answer:", best)
print(2 ** 100)
